Please answer this question with a number--which of the following best apply to the design in the study: 
        (1) totally fun first (i.e., Entertainment game reappropriated), 
        (2) mostly fun first (i.e., design workshop with disabled stakeholders),
        (3) both fun and utility first (i.e., design workshop with diverse stakeholders), 
        (4) mostly utility first (i.e., primary utilitarian mechanic designed first),
        (5) totally utility first (i.e., made by clinicians or specialists, fun incorporated later)
reasoning: The system was conceived to reinforce basic skills (numbers, letters, money) for adults with developmental disabilities, motivated by gaps in existing educational apps. Design activities (personas, prototypes, focus groups) centered on usability, accessibility, appropriateness, and reinforcement of utilitarian skills, with fun elements (e.g., favorite sports images as positive reinforcers) added to support engagement rather than as the primary goal. Stakeholders included service organizations and caregivers, not a broad entertainment-focused group, indicating a primarily utilitarian design with engagement layered on, matching 'mostly utility first'.

Please answer this question with a number--which of the following best apply to the design in the study: 
        (1) entirely turn-based (i.e., tic tac toe),
        (2) follows a set of steps (i.e., viticulture's dynamic turn ordering),
        (3) turns are taken, but some actions can be taken at any time (i.e., pandemic),
        (4) most actions can be taken at any time, but there are some phases (i.e., PvP death reset timer),
        (5) entirely simultaneous (i.e., race)
reasoning: The study evaluates single-user iPad educational activities (Colors, Money, Numbers, Shapes, Letters, Money Addition). Participants respond to prompts, with progress shown in rounds and responses logged; there is no indication of simultaneous or real-time overlapping actions, phases, or between-player dynamics. Interaction is essentially sequential: user receives a prompt, makes a selection, gets feedback, then proceeds to the next, which best matches an entirely turn-based structure.
